sections.html:
Massachusetts' capital and largest city sits in Suffolk County. Its Office of Neighborhood Services recognizes 23 neighborhoods, and where your house is matters more to a buyer than the word Boston.

Part of the cityNeighborhoods
Downtown coreDowntown or Financial District, Beacon Hill, West End, North End, Chinatown, Bay Village
Central and waterfrontBack Bay, South End, Seaport District, South Boston, East Boston, Charlestown
West and southwestAllston, Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore, Mission Hill, Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, Hyde Park
SouthRoxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan

The city has 53 ZIP codes, so check the ZIP and the neighborhood on your assessment record instead of assuming they match.

Boston was settled in 1625 and became a city in 1822. More than two thirds of inner Boston's modern land did not exist at the founding. It was made by filling tidal areas. That history shows in the houses: Back Bay has single family homes and wooden and brick multi-family row houses, the South End Historic District is the largest surviving contiguous Victorian era neighborhood in the country, and downtown and South Boston mix low rise masonry buildings with modern towers.

If your house is in a historic district such as the South End, ask the city whether review rules apply to exterior work before you plan any repairs.

Boston is the most densely populated state capital in the country, at about 13,977 people per square mile of land. Around 1.2 million people may be inside city limits during work hours. For a seller, on-street parking, building access and noise are real selling points or objections, and buyers will ask about them on a walkthrough.

Boston has hot, humid summers and cold, stormy winters, with occasional periods of heavy snow. The freezing window runs from about November 9 to April 5. Winters can bring wide swings, and the immediate coast often sees rain where inland areas see snow. Expect buyers to ask about the roof, windows and heating. Brick and masonry buildings with old mortar, and wooden row houses with aging porches, show weather damage in different ways, so a recent repair record helps you answer questions. If you have invoices for roof or heating work, keep them with your other sale paperwork.

Values are set as of January 1 before the fiscal year. If you think yours is too high, the first move is an abatement application to the city's assessors. It is due by the date the first actual tax bill comes due, which is generally February 1 where billing is quarterly.

Appeals go next to the Appellate Tax Board, which sits at 100 Cambridge Street at Government Center and often hears cases by video. A typical single family hearing lasts one to two hours, and getting to one can take four months to a year.

Call the Boston Assessing Department for the current rate, to ask whether your home qualifies for the residential exemption, and to confirm your abatement deadline. Your actual bill states the due dates.

Suffolk County Registry of Deeds records your deed, since Boston is in Suffolk County. A deed excise tax is charged at recording. Norfolk County's registry lists $2.28 per $500 of the price or fraction of it, and the same state statute covers Suffolk, so get the Suffolk fee schedule from the registry or your attorney.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department issues a certificate of compliance. Book the inspection the day a closing date is set, and expect a fee.
  • Attorney. Lender-side closings need an attorney's real involvement, which is why most sales use a real estate attorney.
  • Home inspection. Under 760 CMR 74, a seller of certain residential properties cannot make an offer depend on the buyer waiving an inspection.
  • Title systems. Most parcels are recorded land. A few are registered land with a Land Court certificate.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs a notification service that emails you when a document is recorded against your property. It is useful for an inherited home or any house with a title question.

Plenty of Boston houses hold more than one unit. If yours does, the city's Inspectional Services Department can tell you whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and your attorney can explain how leases pass to a buyer.

A direct sale lets you skip showings while tenants stay in place. Cash Home Buyers buys Boston houses as they are, and you can compare our number with a listing price before you decide.

Most delays in a Boston sale come from documents, not buyers. Start with the ones only you can find: the deed, your latest tax bill, any permit records for work done on the house, and a list of repairs you know about. If a relative owned the house before you, add the probate paperwork. If tenants live there, add every lease.

Then check what the city already has. The Assessing Department can tell you how your property is classified and whether a residential exemption is on file. Inspectional Services can tell you about rental registration. The registry holds the recorded history of your title, and the notification service mentioned above will tell you if anything new is filed against it.

Put the contacts and answers in one folder. Your attorney and any buyer, cash or otherwise, will ask for the same items, and having them ready shortens the days between an agreement and a closing.

Older Boston houses often need work that a mortgage lender will flag, such as roofs, heating, wiring or egress. Fixing them before a listing costs money and time, and parking, access and noise already test a buyer's patience. Selling as-is to Cash Home Buyers puts that work on us. You still handle the tax payoff, the alarm certificate and the deed recording, but you skip staging, open houses and a buyer's financing contingency.

1. Find your latest tax bill and note its due dates and any exemption on it.
  2. Call the Assessing Department about your abatement deadline and the residential exemption.
  3. Confirm your neighborhood and ZIP on the assessment record.
  4. Schedule the fire department certificate once a closing date is set.
  5. Choose a real estate attorney and ask about the Suffolk registry fees.
  6. Gather your mortgage statement, if one remains, so the payoff can be confirmed before closing day.
  7. Ask your attorney who will pay for the fire department inspection, you or the buyer, and put the answer in writing.
  8. If tenants live there, gather the leases and ask Inspectional Services about rental registration.

With a traditional sale, a buyer's lender adds an appraisal and a loan approval to this list. A cash sale drops them, and the house is bought in its current condition.

faqs.q: How many neighborhoods does Boston have?
faqs.a: The city's Office of Neighborhood Services designates 23, including Back Bay, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, South Boston and the North End.
Suffolk County. Deeds for Boston property are recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Boston property tax assessment?
faqs.a: Start with an abatement application to the Boston assessors, due by the first actual bill's due date. A denial or no answer gives you three months to go to the Appellate Tax Board.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell a Boston house?
faqs.a: Yes, for a one or two family home. The local fire department must certify that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Boston house that has tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask Inspectional Services whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and ask your attorney how the leases transfer to a buyer.
